newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters strike UPS, no end seen anytime soon.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters strike UPS, no end seen anytime soon.

text.p: The Teamsters union went on strike at United Parcel Service on Monday, crippling the nation's largest package delivery company and creating headaches for millions of businesses and consumers.
Striking drivers, package-sorters and loaders shut down UPS facilities across the country after midnight, just hours after talks collapsed in a dispute over pay, benefits and job security.
UPS handles 12 million packages a day, or about 80 percent of domestic parcel deliveries. It employs 301,000 workers in the United States, 185,000 of them Teamsters.
The company, based in Atlanta, and the union blamed each other for the strike, which began early on Monday after the federally mediated talks broke off late on Sunday.

"I think working people have been taking it on the chin long enough and I just think working people in this country are saying 'Enough is enough,'" Teamsters President Ron Carey told CNN. "It's a crime that they have forced our members into a strike."

Chief UPS negotiator Dave Murray called the union's decision to abandon the talks "highly irresponsible" and said the union's leadership should let its members review the company's "last, best and final offer," made last week.
Carey said the union was particularly concerned about preventing work from going to subcontractors rather than union workers, as welll as pension benefits and health and safety issues.
President Clinton said he would not intervene and urged the parties to try to settle the walkout, which disrupted shipping plans for businesses and consumers across the country.

"UPS is a very important company to our country and there are a lot of employees there and I hope they'll go back to the table," Clinton told reporters. "At this time I don't think any further action by me is appropriate."
Murray said UPS was "doing what it can" to keep operations going and was trying to ensure that blood, hospital equipment and other packages with critical supplies reach their destinations.
Rival shippers, including Federal Express Corp., reported a sharp pickup in business.

The Postal Service said it was limiting how many parcels customers could mail at once and taking other steps to handle an expected big increase in the volume of parcel mail, Postmaster General Marvin Runyon said in a statement.
UPS said last week that the threat of a strike was costing it about $5 million a day in business lost to competitors such as the Postal Service and Federal Express.
Union workers were picketing or getting ready to picket outside about 1,700 UPS hub and shipping facilities and at airports where the company maintains air-delivery operations.
"We're striking for every worker in America. We can't have only low service-industry wages in this country," Randy Walls, a 47-year-old UPS driver, said in Atlanta.
The Independent Pilots Association said its 2,000 UPS pilots would refuse work.

Carey said the union was ready for a fight. "We will do whatever it takes to win this, to bring that to the company's attention, and that's what this is about," he said on ABC's "Good Morning America."

UPS said the vast majority of Teamster workers were out on strike and that it was sticking to its final offer. UPS offered to boost pay for both full- and part-time workers by as much as $2.50 an hour over five years.
With revenue of $22.4 billion in 1996, UPS annually handles 3 billion parcels and documents, shipped to countries around the world.
